newsitem.title: USA: Committee to act on constitutional amendments.
newsitem.headline: Committee to act on constitutional amendments.

text.p: The House Judiciary Committee will consider several proposed constitutional amendments, including ones to grant rights to crime victims and limit congressional terms, Chairman Henry Hyde said Wednesday.

Hyde, in a statement outlining the committee's agenda for the two-year session of Congress that began Tuesday, said the panel would also act on bills to limit liability damages, extend copyright protection to material on the Internet and ban the procedure that opponents call partial-birth abortions.
President Clinton last year vetoed bills passed by the Republican-controlled Congress on the abortion procedure and product liability limits.

Hyde also said the committee would review the operations of the FBI, the Immigration and Naturalisation Service and the federal courts, which are under its jurisdiction. Republicans have a 20-15 majority on the committee.
"As was the case in the last Congress, the Judiciary Committee will be very active on a wide range of issues that touch the lives of virutally every American," the Illinois Republican said.

Constitutional amendments must be passed by a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate in order to be sent to the states for ratification. Several were considered in the last session of Congress but none passed.

Among these was one limiting House and Senate members to 12-year terms, which failed in both chambers. Hyde was one of the opponents, arguing that term limits would restrict the choice of voters and force out many of the most capable members. Supporters said term limits would make Congress more responsive to voters and reduce the power of senior members.

Another proposed amendment that passed the House and failed by only one vote in the Senate would require Congress to pass a balanced federal budget each year. It is given a good chance of passage this year.
The victims' rights amendment would give crime victims the right to confront their attackers in court and provide them with restitution.

The partial birth abortion bill would ban abortions in the last two-thirds of a pregnancy unless the life of the mother was in danger. Clinton said he might sign a modified bill if it provided more protection for mothers.

He vetoed the bill limiting product liability damages, which was supported by many Democrats as well as Republicans, saying it went too far in restricting the rights of accident victims to get compensation.
